'''''Hibbertia empetrifolia''''', commonly known as '''trailing guinea-flower''',<ref name="ANBG">{{cite web |last1=Ollerenshaw |first1=Peter |title=''Hibbertia empetrifolia'' |url=http://www.anbg.gov.au/gnp/gnp10/hibbertia-empetrifolia.html |publisher=Australian National Botanic Gardens |access-date=3 June 2021}}</ref> is a species of flowering plant in the family [[Dilleniaceae]] and is [[endemic]] to south-eastern Australia. It is a low-lying to spreading shrub with wiry stems, oblong to lance-shaped leaves with the narrower end towards the base, and pale to bright yellow flowers arranged on the ends of branchlets, with five to nine [[stamen]]s arranged on one side of the two [[Gynoecium#Carpels|carpels]].

==Description==
''Hibbertia empetrifolia'' is a low-lying to spreading shrub with trailing to wiry stems and that typically grows to a height of {{cvt|60|cm}}. The leaves are oblong to lance-shaped with the narrower end towards the base, {{cvt|5–7|mm}} long and {{cvt|1–3|mm}} wide with the edges turned down or rolled under. Both surfaces of the leaves have simple, hooked or star-shaped hairs. The flowers are arranged singly on the ends of branchlets on a [[Peduncle (botany)|peduncle]] {{cvt|2–10|mm}} long. The [[sepal]]s are {{cvt|3–5|mm}} long and the petals yellow and {{cvt|3–6|mm}} long. There are between five and nine stamens arranged on one side of the two carpels. Flowering occurs in most months.<ref name="RBGS">{{cite web |title=''Hibbertia empetrifolia'' |url=https://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/NSWfl.pl?page=nswfl&lvl=sp&name=Hibbertia~empetrifolia |publisher=Royal Botanic Garden Sydney |access-date=3 June 2021}}</ref><ref name="RBGV">{{cite web |last1=Messina |first1=Andre |last2=Stajsic |first2=Val |title=''Hibbertia empetrifolia'' subsp. ''empetrifolia'' |url=https://vicflora.rbg.vic.gov.au/flora/taxon/76d78236-972c-4178-ac03-ede1fbde0397 |publisher=Royal Botanic Gardens Victoria |access-date=3 June 2021}}</ref><ref name="JABG">{{cite journal |last1=Toelken |first1=Hellmut R. |title=Notes on ''Hibbertia'' (Dilleniaceae) 2. The ''H. aspera'' - ''empetrifolia'' complex |journal=Journal of the Adelaide Botanic Gardens |date=1998 |volume=18 |issue=2 |pages=137–144 |url=https://data.environment.sa.gov.au/Content/Publications/JABG18P107_Toelken.pdf |access-date=3 June 2021}}</ref><ref name=Viridans>{{cite book |title=Wild Plants of Victoria (database)|year=2009 |publisher=Viridans Biological Databases & Department of Sustainability and Environment}}</ref>

==Taxonomy==
This species was first formally described in 1817 by Swiss botanist [[Augustin Pyramus de Candolle]] in his book, ''Regni Vegetabilis Systema Naturale'' and was given the name ''Pleurandra empetrifolia''.<ref name=APNI1>{{cite web|title=''Pleurandra empetrifolia''|url= http://id.biodiversity.org.au/instance/apni/503181 |publisher=APNI|access-date=3 June 2021}}</ref><ref name="DC.">{{cite book |last1=de Candolle |first1=Augustin Pyramus |title=Regni Vegetabilis Systema Naturale |volume=1 |date=1817 |location=Paris |page=420 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/127665#page/430/mode/1up |access-date=3 June 2021}}</ref> In 1974, [[Ruurd Dirk Hoogland]] changed the name to ''Hibbertia empetrifolia'' in the ''[[Kew Bulletin]]''.<ref name=APNI>{{cite web|title=''Hibbertia empetrifolia''|url= http://id.biodiversity.org.au/instance/apni/503181 |publisher=APNI|access-date=3 June 2021}}</ref> The [[Binomial nomenclature|specific epithet]] (''empetrifolia'') refers to a similarity of the leaves to those in the genus ''[[Empetrum]]''.<ref name="ANBG" />

In 1998, [[Hellmut R. Toelken]] described three subspecies in the ''[[Journal of the Adelaide Botanic Gardens]]'', and the names of two are accepted by the [[Australian Plant Census]]:<ref name="JABG" />
* ''Hibbertia empetrifolia'' <small>(DC.) Hoogland</small> subsp. ''empetrifolia'';<ref name=APC1>{{cite web|title=''Hibbertia empetrifolia'' subsp. ''empetrifolia''|url= https://biodiversity.org.au/nsl/services/apc-format/display/171279|publisher=Australian Plant Census|access-date=3 June 2021}}</ref> 
* ''Hibbertia empetrifolia'' subsp. ''radians'' <small>Toelken</small><ref name=APC2>{{cite web|title=''Hibbertia empetrifolia'' subsp. ''radians''|url= https://biodiversity.org.au/nsl/services/apc-format/display/171286|publisher=Australian Plant Census|access-date=3 June 2021}}</ref> that differs from the [[Autonym (botany)|autonym]] in having star-shaped hairs with fewer branches.<ref name="JABG" />

==Distribution and habitat==
This guinea-flower occurs from south-east Queensland, through New South Wales and Victoria to [[Kangaroo Island]] in South Australia and in Tasmania. It grows in woodland and forest, scrambling over other vegetation. Subspecies ''empetrifolia'' is found on the coast and tablelands of New South Wales, coastal areas of Victoria east of [[Port Phillip Bay]], the east coast of Tasmania. Subspecies ''radians'' only occurs in south-eastern South Australia.<ref name="ANBG" /><ref name="RBGS" /><ref name="RBGV" /><ref name="JABG" /><ref name="utas">{{cite web |last1=Jordan |first1=Greg |title=''Hibbertia empetrifolia'' |url=https://www.utas.edu.au/dicotkey/dicotkey/DILLEN/SHibbertia_empetrifolia.htm |publisher=University of Tasmania |access-date=3 June 2021}}</ref>

==Use in horticulture==
''Hibbertia empetrifolia'' is regarded as one of the best suited species of ''Hibbertia'' for cultivation in gardens, preferring a well-drained situation with some shade. It is frost resistant and withstands some dryness, but performs best with adequate moisture.<ref name=Greig>{{cite book|author=Greig, D.| title=The Australian Gardener's Wildflower Catalogue| publisher=Angus & Robertson|location= Australia | year=1987 | isbn=0207154600}}</ref>
